title: Suffix Array (Basics)
tagline: All suffixes sorted — compact substring search and the base for LCP-powered string magic.

intuition.analogy: Imagine listing every suffix of a word and sorting them alphabetically, like dictionary entries. Once sorted, finding any substring is a binary search — and neighbouring entries reveal how much consecutive suffixes have in common.
paragraphs: A suffix array is the sorted order of all suffixes of a string, stored as their starting indices. It's a memory-light alternative to a suffix tree that still enables powerful substring queries.

The naive build sorts n suffixes in O(n² log n). The standard prefix-doubling method sorts by first 1, then 2, 4, 8… characters using ranks from the previous round, reaching O(n log n) (or O(n log² n) with simple sorting).

Paired with the LCP (Longest Common Prefix) array — the overlap between adjacent sorted suffixes — it answers 'number of distinct substrings', 'longest repeated substring', and pattern counting efficiently.
intuition.keyIdea: Sort suffixes by doubling the compared length each round, reusing previous ranks for O(n log n).

steps.title: Rank by first character
steps.detail: Initial ranks are the characters themselves.

steps.title: Prefix doubling
steps.detail: For k = 1, 2, 4, …, sort suffixes by the pair (rank[i], rank[i+k]); recompute ranks from the sorted order.

steps.title: Build LCP (Kasai)
steps.detail: Using the inverse permutation, compute adjacent LCPs in O(n) by reusing the previous suffix's overlap minus one.

codes.source:
def suffix_array(s):                  # O(n log^2 n) prefix doubling
    n = len(s)
    sa = list(range(n))
    rank = [ord(c) for c in s]
    tmp = [0] * n
    k = 1
    while k < n:
        def key(i):
            return (rank[i], rank[i + k] if i + k < n else -1)
        sa.sort(key=key)
        tmp[sa[0]] = 0
        for i in range(1, n):
            tmp[sa[i]] = tmp[sa[i-1]] + (key(sa[i-1]) < key(sa[i]))
        rank = tmp[:]
        k <<= 1
    return sa

complexity.time: O(n log n) to O(n log² n)
complexity.timeReason: log n doubling rounds, each sorting/radix-sorting the suffixes.

pitfalls: Use a sentinel/end handling so comparisons of unequal-length suffixes are well-defined.
Radix sort the pairs for true O(n log n); comparison sort gives O(n log² n).
The LCP array (Kasai's algorithm) is what unlocks most applications — don't skip it.

problems.title: Longest Repeated Substring
problems.statement: Find the longest substring that appears at least twice.
problems.hint: Max value in the LCP array.

approach: Build the suffix array (suffixes sorted) and the LCP array (longest common prefix of adjacent suffixes).
Two equal substrings appear as a shared prefix of adjacent sorted suffixes, so the longest repeated substring length is max(LCP).

problems.title: Number of Distinct Substrings
problems.statement: Count distinct substrings of a string.

approach: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix. The total number of prefixes is n(n+1)/2, but adjacent sorted suffixes share LCP-many prefixes that are duplicates.

problems.title: Longest Duplicate Substring
problems.statement: Longest substring occurring more than once.
problems.hint: Suffix array + LCP (or binary search + hashing).

approach: The longest duplicated substring is the maximum LCP between adjacent sorted suffixes — identical to the longest repeated substring.
Build the suffix array and LCP; return the substring achieving max LCP.

problems.title: Pattern Matching via SA
problems.hint: Binary search the suffix array for the pattern range.

approach: Sorted suffixes let us binary-search a pattern: all suffixes starting with the pattern form a contiguous block.
Find the lower and upper bounds by comparing the pattern with suffix prefixes; the matching suffix start indices are the occurrence positions.

problems.title: Lexicographically Smallest Rotation
problems.hint: Build SA of s+s; first valid suffix gives the rotation.

approach: The lexicographically smallest rotation is found by Booth's algorithm on the doubled string in linear time.
It scans s+s maintaining the candidate start of the least rotation, advancing past mismatches like a failure-function comparison.
